video_title: Could AI Break Cryptography Soon? Yes, but 'Bunker Mode' May Not Be the Solution
gist: Project 11's Alex Pruden and Connor Deegan assess Justin Drake's 'bunker mode' warning that AI could break elliptic-curve cryptography before quantum computers do: AI has already broken two non-production schemes, but no production scheme is broken today. They argue the hashes-vs-lattices debate matters less than starting crypto-agile post-quantum migration now, put earliest quantum Q-day around 2030 (likely 2033-35), and pitch their Strongpoint custody platform with Realm insurance.

themes.theme: AI as a new attack vector on cryptography

insights.claim: Project 11's CTO argues the AI threat to cryptography is already live: AI has broken two non-production schemes in the last two months, making the 'AI day' more immediate than quantum Q-day.
insights.speaker: Connor Deegan (Project 11 CTO)
insights.so_what: Crypto security risk is no longer just a 2030s quantum story; AI-driven cryptanalysis is a near-term tail risk for chains and custodians.

insights.claim: Two candidate cryptographic schemes, the lattice-based Hawk and another algebraically structured scheme ('Mac'), fell to AI-assisted attacks in the past two months; one break reportedly cost about $100,000 using Anthropic's model, and neither was used in production.
insights.speaker: Connor Deegan (Project 11 CTO)
insights.so_what: Cheap AI cryptanalysis lowers the cost of attacking new or structured schemes; scrutinize any protocol adopting young cryptography.

insights.claim: Public-key cryptography rests on math problems believed but not proven hard, so OpenAI releasing hundreds of solved math results raised fears that AI could find hidden structure in trapdoor functions like elliptic curves.
insights.speaker: Alex Pruden (Project 11 CEO)
insights.so_what: Advances in AI math capability are a leading indicator for cryptographic risk to blockchains, banks and TLS alike.

insights.claim: Schemes with rich algebraic structure (elliptic curves, lattices, isogenies) are seen as more exposed to AI attack than hash-based schemes, because AI excels at finding errors in human mathematics.
insights.speaker: Connor Deegan (Project 11 CTO)
insights.so_what: Useful lens for ranking which chains' signature choices carry more AI-era tail risk.

insights.claim: Despite the debate, no known attack exists today on elliptic curves, the NIST lattice schemes or hash-based post-quantum schemes; Bitcoin and Ethereum will rely on elliptic curves for at least two more years before any migration.
insights.speaker: Connor Deegan (Project 11 CTO)
insights.so_what: Counters panic narratives; any 'ECDSA broken' headline should be treated skeptically absent a published break.
insights.quote: none of these schemes are broken today

insights.claim: Speculation that AI labs are hiding cryptographic breaks was fueled by gaps in the numbering of OpenAI's released math problems (jumping from problem 44 to 47), which may simply be a typo.
insights.speaker: Connor Deegan (Project 11 CTO)
insights.so_what: Information asymmetry: frontier labs may know about breaks before the market; monitor lab disclosures for anomalies.

insights.claim: Quantum computing labs have confirmed they are withholding some results from publication, either because they were told to or to avoid causing panic.
insights.speaker: Alex Pruden (Project 11 CEO)
insights.so_what: Public quantum progress likely understates true capability, arguing for earlier rather than later migration.

themes.theme: Bunker mode: Justin Drake vs Yehuda Lindell

insights.claim: Ethereum researcher Justin Drake proposed 'bunker mode', a controlled mass migration of assets to fresh addresses whose public keys stay hidden behind a hash, citing AI progress in math; Project 11 calls the hashed-address part sound advice.
insights.speaker: Connor Deegan (Project 11 CTO)
insights.so_what: Holders can cut exposure now by keeping coins in addresses that have never revealed a public key.

insights.claim: Project 11's Bitcoin risk list tracks how much Bitcoin sits in addresses with exposed public keys, which is vulnerable to quantum attack.
insights.speaker: Connor Deegan (Project 11 CTO)
insights.so_what: The exposed-key BTC supply is a watchable metric of how much supply is at risk of theft in a Q-day or AI-break event.

insights.claim: Coinbase head of cryptography Yehuda Lindell rebutted Drake, saying there is no evidence of a break in decades-old hardness assumptions like elliptic curve cryptography, and that historically hash functions have been broken more often than elliptic curves.
insights.speaker: host (quoting Yehuda Lindell)
insights.so_what: Major custodians are unlikely to rush away from ECDSA; expect institutional resistance to hash-only migrations.

insights.claim: Elliptic curves are the only cryptographic schemes guarding a trillion-dollar honeypot, so their survival since Bitcoin's launch is the strongest real-world test any cryptography has passed.
insights.speaker: Connor Deegan (Project 11 CTO)
insights.so_what: ECDSA's track record is a reason against panic-driven migrations to less battle-tested schemes.
insights.quote: They are the only cryptographic schemes that have a trillion dollar asset honeypot.

insights.claim: The Drake-Lindell split reflects incentives: a protocol designer is optimizing Ethereum for 30 to 100 years and dreads slow upgrades like ETH1 to ETH2, while Coinbase's cryptographer is responsible for billions in custody today and won't discard proven cryptography.
insights.speaker: Alex Pruden (Project 11 CEO)
insights.so_what: Read cryptographers' public stances through their institutional incentives; expect lattice camps to back lattices and hash camps to back hashes.

insights.claim: Historically more hash functions have been retired than standard elliptic curve schemes, usually because outputs were found to be less random than required.
insights.speaker: Connor Deegan (Project 11 CTO)
insights.so_what: Hash-based schemes are not risk-free; pick specific battle-tested hashes.

insights.claim: Hash functions like SHA-256 are arguably heavily battle-tested because Bitcoin mining computes astronomically many hashes and any miner who found a pattern would profit enormously, though ad-hoc proof-of-work hashes are broken all the time.
insights.speaker: Alex Pruden (Project 11 CEO)
insights.so_what: Bitcoin mining economics act as a continuous bounty on SHA-256; favor chains built on mainstream hashes over bespoke ones.

themes.theme: Hashes vs lattices for post-AI security

insights.claim: Justin Drake favors going all-in on hash-based cryptography (e.g., SHA or Blake families) and avoiding curves, lattices and isogenies, while StarkWare's Eli Ben-Sasson argues succinct lattice schemes based on module SIS (around since 2012) need another 3 to 5 years of AI scrutiny before securing serious money.
insights.speaker: host (quoting Justin Drake and Eli Ben-Sasson)
insights.so_what: Lattice-based roadmaps (backed by a16z's 'case for lattices') carry a contested young-cryptography risk.

insights.claim: NIST standardized both a lattice-based and a hash-based post-quantum signature scheme but recommends the lattice scheme ML-DSA as primary, largely because hash-based signatures are bigger and slower.
insights.speaker: Alex Pruden (Project 11 CEO)
insights.so_what: Performance costs (size, speed, gas) are why chains may not go hash-only, affecting throughput and fees.

insights.claim: Structured cryptography allows scaffolding like multi-party computation (used by custodians such as Fireblocks), which random hash-based schemes cannot support, so a hash-only world would disrupt MPC custody.
insights.speaker: Alex Pruden (Project 11 CEO)
insights.so_what: MPC custody providers face redesign costs if the industry shifts to hash-based signatures; watch custody vendors' post-quantum roadmaps.

insights.claim: Blockchains will move from a single elliptic-curve standard to a multipolar world where different users and chains pick lattices, hashes or other schemes, creating uncharted interoperability and infrastructure complexity.
insights.speaker: Alex Pruden (Project 11 CEO)
insights.so_what: Fragmentation of signature schemes creates opportunity for wallet, custody and infrastructure firms that support many algorithms.

insights.claim: Vitalik Buterin noted signatures and proofs can already go hash-only, but public-key encryption has no hash-based equivalent; Project 11 says this mainly threatens privacy protocols such as Zcash, where a break would retroactively reveal activity rather than steal funds.
insights.speaker: Alex Pruden (Project 11 CEO)
insights.so_what: Privacy coins carry distinct long-term risk, since past encrypted activity could be exposed if key-exchange cryptography falls.

insights.claim: Project 11 warns that months spent on ego battles over lattices versus hashes distract from migration work; picking a signature scheme is only one of thousands of decisions needed.
insights.speaker: Connor Deegan (Project 11 CTO)
insights.so_what: Judge chains by migration progress, not by which scheme camp they join.

themes.theme: Can blockchains survive a crypto break?

insights.claim: Haseeb Qureshi of Dragonfly argues that banks, TLS and certificate authorities can recover from a public-key break by reissuing keys, but blockchains cannot, because anyone could compute anyone's keys and ownership would be unprovable.
insights.speaker: host (quoting Haseeb Qureshi)
insights.so_what: Undercuts the 'if ECDSA breaks we all have bigger problems' complacency; crypto assets carry unique, unhedgeable tail risk.
insights.quote: That's no longer a currency. That's a graffiti wall.

insights.claim: Alex Pruden thinks blockchains could recover socially through forks, as Ethereum did after the DAO re-entrancy bug and the ETH Classic split, provided usable cryptography exists for the new fork.
insights.speaker: Alex Pruden (Project 11 CEO)
insights.so_what: A cryptographic break might be a disruptive fork event rather than a zero for major chains, a key assumption for tail-risk sizing.

insights.claim: Blockchains are uniquely exposed because nothing stands between a valid signature and moving money, unlike banks that can flag suspicious wires; Satoshi's coins could be moved by whoever obtains the private key.
insights.speaker: Alex Pruden (Project 11 CEO)
insights.so_what: Permissionlessness is both the product and the vulnerability; dormant early coins with exposed keys are the obvious first target.

insights.claim: Dankrad Feist argued that if elliptic curves break so every exposed public key is compromised, coins go to zero regardless of bunker mode; the host calls this a nihilist view.
insights.speaker: host (quoting Dankrad Feist)
insights.so_what: Shows how far apart informed views are on whether an ECDSA break would be survivable for crypto prices.

insights.claim: Alex Pruden puts the earliest realistic quantum attack around 2030 and the more-likely-than-not window at 2033 to 2035, with recent error-correction results making the earlier end more likely.
insights.speaker: Alex Pruden (Project 11 CEO)
insights.so_what: Sets the planning horizon for Bitcoin and Ethereum post-quantum migrations; exposure should be resolved before ~2030.

insights.claim: Google's magic-states result and an error-correction result from Quantinuum show real engineering progress in quantum computing and weaken the 'it's all just theory' skeptic argument, though they do not move Q-day estimates much.
insights.speaker: Alex Pruden (Project 11 CEO)
insights.so_what: Steady quantum hardware milestones are a reason to price in a post-quantum transition rather than dismiss it.

insights.claim: Justin Drake said it is reasonable to brace for ECDSA breaking before Q-day, in the worst case within months, meaning fast private-key recovery within a week on a large GPU cluster; Project 11's CTO does not expect elliptic curves to break in the next couple of months.
insights.speaker: Connor Deegan (Project 11 CTO)
insights.so_what: Tail-scenario framing; low-probability but catastrophic risk for exposed-key coins.

insights.claim: Post-quantum and post-AI migration are the same work: moving to a hash-based scheme would cover both threats, so starting a post-quantum migration now also hedges the AI risk.
insights.speaker: Connor Deegan (Project 11 CTO)
insights.so_what: Chains with active post-quantum roadmaps also reduce AI-break risk, a selection criterion for long-term holdings.

insights.claim: Project 11 argues crypto agility (supporting several signature schemes so any one can be swapped out) will define the future of blockchain and cybersecurity, with redundancy cost treated like an insurance decision.
insights.speaker: Alex Pruden (Project 11 CEO)
insights.so_what: Favors protocols and custodians built to swap algorithms; redundancy adds cost that must be weighed against secured value.

insights.claim: If systems are built to be agile, AI will also produce new, faster, more gas-efficient cryptography that chains can keep migrating to, so the first post-quantum scheme Bitcoin or Ethereum adopts will not be the last.
insights.speaker: Connor Deegan (Project 11 CTO)
insights.so_what: AI is also a source of better cryptography; agile chains can capture performance gains over time.

insights.claim: Alex Pruden calls the belief that Bitcoin is perfect and will last unchanged forever a fantasy, and bets on chains that are actively doing something over those that do nothing, which he says will face catastrophic consequences.
insights.speaker: Alex Pruden (Project 11 CEO)
insights.so_what: Governance speed on quantum migration is a differentiator; Bitcoin's ossification culture is a risk factor.
insights.quote: choosing to do nothing, I absolutely think will have catastrophic consequences

insights.claim: Haseeb Qureshi's 'cryptographic wartime' plan has every chain deploy a simple hash-based backup key that apps make mandatory, plus a pre-deployed validator-voted kill switch forcing addresses into recovery mode; Balaji Srinivasan suggested opt-in rollback terms and AI agents with token budgets that probe chains for vulnerabilities.
insights.speaker: host (quoting Haseeb Qureshi and Balaji Srinivasan)
insights.so_what: Shows the range of emergency governance designs that could appear in chain roadmaps.

insights.claim: Project 11 says the hard part is building consensus across ecosystems rather than designing fixes; cross-chain mandates like universal rollbacks or token budgets are unrealistic, and 80% of the work is simply starting migration.
insights.speaker: Alex Pruden (Project 11 CEO)
insights.so_what: Expect chain-by-chain, uneven post-quantum readiness; assess each ecosystem's governance capacity separately.

insights.claim: Project 11 launched Strongpoint, a crypto-agile institutional custody platform supporting lattice, hash-based and other post-quantum algorithms, with the Zcash Foundation as design partner and Zcash supported at launch.
insights.speaker: Alex Pruden (Project 11 CEO)
insights.so_what: Early commercial product for post-quantum custody; a signal that institutional demand for quantum-safe custody is forming.

insights.claim: Project 11 is partnering with digital-asset insurer Realm to price quantum and AI cryptographic risk, arguing crypto-agile, post-quantum setups could lower insurance premiums that would otherwise rise.
insights.speaker: Alex Pruden (Project 11 CEO)
insights.so_what: If insurers start pricing cryptographic agility, post-quantum readiness becomes a measurable cost advantage for custodians.
